These are comparable to the U.S. BD price of $3.08–3.73/gallon and the California RD price of $3.10–3.76/gallon in 2020 (DOE, 2025). Modeled MFSPs of other emerging RD pathways range from $3.47 to $4.65 per DGE. Among these emerging pathways, RDs from woody biomass CFP and wet waste HTL pathways have relatively lower MFSPs due to their significant byproduct credits and savings from avoided waste treatment tipping fees. The modeled MFSPs for CFP bio-oil and HTL biocrude are considerably lower than those for CFP RD and HTL RD, primarily because they do not require the upgrading step for bio-oil or biocrude. Notably, the biocrude generated from the sewage sludge HTL pathway has the lowest MFSP of all alternative fuel pathways, $2.05 per DGE. However, the properties of CFP bio-oil and HTL biocrude are also considerably different from petroleum-derived diesel, which limits their potential as drop-in fuel for locomotives and their allowable blending ratio. The tradeoff between the cost of hydroprocessing and developing drop-in fuel such as RD is apparent in the MFSP. Methanol and DME produced from biomass gasification exhibit similar MFSPs, $3.15 and $2.99 per DGE, respectively, because the gasification step has a significant influence on the overall production cost. The MFSP for corn stover ethanol is $4.71 per DGE. This is considerably higher than that of corn ethanol, $3.69 per DGE, due to the lower yield of ethanol from corn stover, higher chemical consumptions and higher capital costs. 7 Figure 2-1 Minimum Fuel Selling Price of Alternative Fuel Pathways, $/Diesel Gallon Equivalent (DGE) (in 2020 USD) In addition, the estimated MFSPs for the two e-fuels—green ammonia and e-methanol produced from renewable hydrogen—are significantly higher than those of other alternative fuels. This is primarily due to the high cost of renewable hydrogen derived from state-of-the-art water electrolysis technology. 2.2.2 Uncertainties in MFSP and Conversion Cost Figure 2-2 illustrates the estimated uncertainties in modeled MFSPs, as well as conversion costs, based on the assumptions summarized in Section 2.1. Here, the conversion cost includes all costs related to production except feedstock cost. Overall, pathways that use first-generation and cellulosic biomass (grey and green boxes in Figure 2-2(a)) have the lowest uncertainties in MFSP (less than ± $1/DGE), because these feedstocks have established markets. Pathways that use waste as feedstock (orange boxes in Figure 2-2(a)) are subjected to slightly higher uncertainties, mainly due to variations in feedstock prices. As expected, commercial pathways (green boxes in Figure 2-2(b)) have the lowest uncertainties in conversion cost, while emerging fuels (orange and grey boxes in Figure 2-2(b)) and emerging RD pathways (yellow boxes in Figure 2-2(b)) have mid- level uncertainties in conversion costs. 8 Figure 2-2 Minimum Fuel Selling Price and Conversion Cost with Uncertainties, $/Diesel Gallon Equivalent (DGE) (in 2020 USD) The uncertainties in MFSPs and conversion costs of soybean-derived BD and RD are comparatively low.
